entities.name: Alexander of Lincoln
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alexander of Lincoln (d. 1148) was a powerful and politically astute English prelate, serving as Bishop of Lincoln from 1123 until his death. A scion of an influential Anglo-Norman ecclesiastical and administrative dynasty, he was nephew to Roger of Salisbury, the formidable Bishop and Chancellor under Henry I, and cousin to Nigel, Bishop of Ely and Treasurer. Alexander distinguished himself as a significant patron of architecture and learning, earning the moniker 'the Magnificent' for his extensive building projects and lavish lifestyle, reflecting the immense wealth and temporal power wielded by high-ranking churchmen in 12th-century England.

His episcopacy was marked by ambitious construction, including the rebuilding and fortification of Lincoln Cathedral after a fire, and the erection of strategic castles at Newark and Sleaford, which underscored his dual role as a spiritual leader and a feudal lord. Educated in the intellectual hub of Laon, Alexander brought a refined sensibility to his diocese, fostering a vibrant cultural environment. However, his political fortunes were inextricably linked to his family's ascendancy and subsequent decline. During the tumultuous period of the Anarchy (1135-1153), his loyalty was questioned by King Stephen, leading to his arrest and imprisonment alongside his uncle Roger and cousin Nigel in 1139, a dramatic event that severely weakened the episcopacy's secular power.
